projects.title: Z-Graph: Interactive Math Visualization Platform
projects.excerpt: An interactive math visualization product built to explore equations, curves, fields, fractals, and surfaces across both 2D and 3D, with live formula editing and immediate visual feedback.
projects.description: Z-Graph is a graphics-heavy React and TypeScript application for exploring mathematical behavior visually instead of treating equations as static text. It combines Cartesian graphs, trigonometric and logarithmic functions, implicit curves, calculus visuals, polar and parametric systems, vector and slope fields, Fourier-style expressions, complex-plane visuals, fractals, parametric surfaces, and implicit 3D surfaces in one consistent interface. I structured it around reusable category definitions, configurable parameters, and worker-assisted computation so the app stays extensible and responsive as the rendering workload gets heavier.
highlights: Supports a wide range of graphing modes including algebra, calculus, polar, parametric, vector-field, fractal, and 3D surface exploration
Live formula editing, presets, parameter controls, animation, fullscreen mode, and PNG export turn equations into interactive systems
Reusable category-based architecture plus worker-assisted computation keeps graphics-heavy visualization maintainable and responsive

projects.title: ZTable: React Native Chemistry Reference App
projects.excerpt: A production-minded Expo and React Native chemistry app that combines a periodic table, localized element detail screens, atom-shell visualization, ion references, and classroom-oriented tools in a cleaner feature-based architecture.
projects.description: ZTable is a React Native chemistry reference and learning app built with Expo, TypeScript, Expo Router, Zustand, and NativeWind. The codebase was heavily refactored to move oversized TSX screens and chemistry utilities into feature-based modules, with thin route shells in `app/`, domain logic in `features/chemistry`, reusable UI in `components/`, and structured translations in `i18n/`. The result is a mobile app that stays readable, scalable, and maintainable while preserving public behavior across the periodic table, localized element profiles, atomic visualization, ion references, worksheets, and chemistry utilities.
highlights: Feature-based refactor split large route components, chemistry logic, and locale files into smaller focused modules
Periodic table, localized element details, atom visualization, ion references, worksheet tooling, and chemistry helpers live behind clearer reusable boundaries
Typecheck, lint, formatting, and Bun-based chemistry tests were stabilized so the refactor improved structure without regressing behavior

projects.title: Whisper Chat: Cross-Platform Real-Time Messaging App
projects.excerpt: A full-stack real-time messaging platform with Expo mobile, React web, and an Express plus Socket.IO backend, built to show production-style chat behavior instead of tutorial-level fake messaging.
projects.description: Whisper Chat is a full-stack TypeScript messaging system with three coordinated parts: a mobile client built with Expo and React Native, a web client built with React and Vite, and a backend API built with Express, Socket.IO, MongoDB, and Mongoose. It uses Clerk for authentication across web, mobile, and backend, TanStack Query for server state, Zustand for transient realtime state, and refactored socket modules for connection state, events, cache updates, unread markers, typing indicators, and online presence. The project focuses on real architecture: authenticated REST plus websocket flows, optimistic message sending, cross-platform product consistency, and maintainable state boundaries.
highlights: Shared backend supports authenticated REST APIs and authenticated websocket connections for both web and mobile clients
Realtime features include one-to-one chat creation, optimistic messaging, typing indicators, online presence, unread state, and chat preview updates
TanStack Query and Zustand are separated by responsibility so server state and realtime UI state stay maintainable as the app grows

projects.title: zsk-react-error: React Error Boundary & Reporter
projects.excerpt: A TypeScript-first React error boundary and reporter package with advanced error state control, reset logic, and analytics integration. Designed for scalable, production-grade error handling in React apps.
projects.description: A robust React error boundary and reporter package supporting both global and local error state, composable hooks, imperative resets, and flexible fallback UI. Integrates easily with Zustand and analytics tools for complete error visibility.
highlights: Global and local error state management with composable hooks
Keyed error isolation and imperative reset support
Customizable fallback UI and error reporting integration
Optimized for performance and scalable error handling
Easy integration with Zustand and analytics tools

projects.title: Smart AI: Full-Stack SaaS AI Platform
projects.excerpt: A comprehensive SaaS platform democratizing access to AI capabilities. Provides features for article generation, image creation/editing, resume analysis, and community interaction—with freemium tier distinction enforced at the API boundary.
projects.description: Full-stack AI-powered SaaS application integrating multiple AI services (Gemini, ClipDrop) and media processing (Cloudinary) with plan-based access control. Features user dashboards, creation history, community feed, and usage tracking.
highlights: Full-stack architecture with Express backend and React frontend
Integrated AI services: Google Gemini (text), ClipDrop (images), Cloudinary (storage)
Plan-based access control enforced server-side with Clerk authentication
User creation history, community feed, and like/publish system
Usage tracking and rate limiting for free tier users
MikroORM for type-safe database operations with PostgreSQL
Comprehensive API routes for AI generation and user management

projects.title: Auto Pause & Media Control: Chrome Extension
projects.excerpt: A zero-dependency Chrome extension that automatically pauses media when you switch tabs and gives you precise scroll-wheel control over volume, playback speed, and scrubbing—no library required, just clean browser APIs.
projects.description: A lightweight, privacy-first Chrome extension built on pure vanilla JavaScript and the Chrome Extensions API. It intelligently pauses audio/video on tab blur and resumes on return, with scroll-wheel shortcuts for volume, speed, and scrubbing. Includes a Glassmorphism popup UI with individual feature toggles and a master kill-switch.
highlights: Smart Auto-Pause: pauses media on tab switch and resumes precisely on return
Precision Media Scrubbing via Shift+Alt+Scroll using smooth trackpad scaling
Master Volume Control with Alt+Scroll hover gesture
Dynamic Playback Speed (0.25x–4.0x) via Ctrl+Alt+Scroll
Glassmorphism popup UI with per-feature toggles and a master power switch
Zero data collected—pure local JavaScript with no external dependencies

projects.title: zsk-portfolio: This Portfolio (over-engineered by design)
projects.excerpt: The site you're looking at right now. Built as a deliberate exercise in senior-level architecture using React 19, Vanilla Extract, Zustand, a zero-runtime CSS design system, and a focused AI resume assistant backed by FastAPI, Groq, and Redis rate limiting.
projects.description: A fully interactive developer portfolio built to showcase architectural decision-making as much as UI craft. Uses a headless JSON data layer, type-safe CSS-in-JS compiled at build time, compound component patterns, PWA offline support, a synthetic Web Audio click engine, hydration-safe state persistence, and an Ask AI experience. The AI feature connects the React frontend to a separate FastAPI backend that reads a structured resume profile JSON, calls Groq with a strict prompt, prioritizes professional experience before project evidence, caches repeated questions with Upstash Redis, and supports IP-based production rate limiting.
highlights: Added an Ask AI portfolio assistant with React chat UI, FastAPI backend, Groq Llama integration, strict prompt rules, and JSON-only responses
Implemented Upstash Redis caching and IP-based rate limiting, with local development bypass and production controls
Reduced LLM token usage by compacting the resume profile before each Groq request and versioning Redis cache keys when prompt behavior changes
Zero-runtime CSS via Vanilla Extract — styles are TypeScript, compiled to static .css at build time
15+ hot-swappable color themes built on a typed createThemeContract design system
React 19 Compiler integration — automatic memoization, no manual useMemo/useCallback
Headless JSON data layer in /public — fully decoupled from the UI, reusable across any future rebuild
Synthetic click sounds via Web Audio API (no .mp3 files, no network requests)
PWA-ready via vite-plugin-pwa with offline service worker caching
Keyboard accessibility: T (theme), M (mute), Cmd+D (download CV)
Custom NPM packages: zsk-react-error and zsk-react-i18n used in production

projects.title: zsk-use-sound: React Hook for File + Generated Sound
projects.excerpt: A TypeScript-first React hook inspired by use-sound that supports both Howler-powered file playback and browser-generated click sounds through one API. Designed for UI feedback without forcing bundled audio assets.
projects.description: zsk-use-sound unifies two sound strategies in one ergonomic hook: file mode for mp3/wav assets via Howler, and generated mode that synthesizes built-in click profiles in the browser when no file is provided. It exposes a familiar tuple API with play controls, mode visibility, and sound-enabled toggling for app-wide mute workflows.
highlights: Dual-mode audio engine: file playback (Howler) and generated Web Audio click presets
TypeScript-first API with exported option/play/control types for consumer safety
Built-in generated profiles (click, soft-click, tick) with volume and playback controls
Supports global mute flow via soundEnabled and per-play override via forceSoundEnabled
use-sound-inspired tuple return shape with stop, pause, duration, and runtime mode metadata

projects.title: zsk-jd: AI-Powered Resume Tailoring Skill
projects.excerpt: A portable LLM skill that performs ATS gap analysis, interview probability scoring, and full LaTeX resume tailoring against any job description — with a mandatory warning gate before output and bilingual cover letter generation.
projects.description: A structured prompt skill for Claude and other LLMs that automates resume tailoring end-to-end: JD parsing, skill gap scoring, ATS keyword injection, and compilable LaTeX output with optional cover letters. Built with strict ATS writing rules, fabrication guardrails, and support for patch-mode diffs.
highlights: Performs weighted skill gap analysis (hard skills 60%, seniority 25%, domain fit 15%) with interview probability estimate
Mandatory warning gate blocks output if match score < 50 or majority of required skills are missing — prevents false confidence
Rewrites professional summary, reorders skills, and injects JD keywords into bullet points without fabricating any experience
Generates standalone compilable LaTeX cover letters in 4 length modes (short, default, long, cover-only) with formal/casual tone flags
Patch mode outputs only changed LaTeX blocks — clean diffs for version control workflows
Strict ATS writing rules: 15+ banned words/phrases, no em dashes, no repetitive bullet structures, no robotic summary openers
Portable across Claude, Cursor, Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini CLI, and any markdown-capable LLM

projects.title: Coin Gate: Live Crypto Market Dashboard
projects.excerpt: A production-style crypto dashboard built with Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript. It combines server-rendered CoinGecko market data with live websocket updates for pricing, trades, OHLC charts, search, and coin conversion in one responsive interface.
projects.description: Coin Gate is a crypto market dashboard built with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Base UI primitives, and lightweight-charts. It includes a home dashboard with featured market views, a paginated coins page, and dynamic coin detail screens with live pricing, recent trades, OHLC charting, and conversion tools. I used server components, client components, route handlers, and websocket subscriptions together so the app can load stable market snapshots first, then layer in live updates without losing responsiveness.
highlights: Home dashboard with featured coin overview, trending assets, and top categories
Paginated coins listing plus dynamic coin pages with live pricing, trades, OHLC charts, and conversion
Shared CoinGecko data layer handling REST, websocket streams, demo/pro API differences, and OHLC fallback logic

projects.title: zperiod: Interactive Chemistry Learning Web App
projects.excerpt: A modern React chemistry console with a searchable periodic table, element profiles, 3D atom visualization, molar mass calculation, equation balancing, ion references, solubility lookup, and worksheet PDF generation.
projects.description: zperiod is a browser-based chemistry learning app built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Bun, TanStack Router, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, vanilla-extract, React Three Fiber, Drei, Three.js, Framer Motion, Vitest, Testing Library, Web Workers, and zsk-react-i18n. It combines a searchable 118-element periodic table with category filters, detailed element profiles, isotope-aware atom visualization, molar mass parsing, equation balancing, common ion references, solubility lookup, and print-ready worksheet generation. The implementation separates pure chemistry logic from React UI, lazy-loads route screens, keeps equation balancing off the main thread, and uses several reasonable optimization techniques without overselling the app as fully optimized.
highlights: Interactive periodic table with search, category filtering, detailed element profiles, common ion data, and localized English/French content
Chemistry tools include molar mass calculation, equation balancing with exact fraction math in a Web Worker, solubility lookup, and worksheet PDF generation
3D atom model uses React Three Fiber, Drei, Three.js, memoized shell helpers, and lazy loading so heavy visual features stay outside the startup path

projects.title: Z Gym: Premium Fitness Brand SPA
projects.excerpt: A production-style fitness SPA built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, and Motion. I treated it like a real frontend system, with scroll-driven sections, reusable UI primitives, typed content, and theme support instead of one-off page styling.
projects.description: Z Gym is a premium fitness brand experience built as a section-based single-page app. It uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI primitives, and Motion for scroll-driven storytelling, responsive layout, and polished dark and light themes. For me, this project is a good example of building more than a modern-looking website. It is also structured to be scalable, reusable, and maintainable, with isolated section components, reusable hooks, shared animation variants, direct imports, and a centralized typed content layer that keeps the codebase held to a high standard.
highlights: Scroll-driven single-page experience with responsive section architecture and premium visual pacing
Reusable UI primitives, shared animation variants, and isolated section components instead of page-specific one-offs
Centralized typed content plus theme support and accessible interactions built for maintainability, not only presentation

projects.title: WC26: Open-Source World Cup 2026 macOS Menu Bar App
projects.excerpt: A small open-source macOS menu bar app built in SwiftUI to track World Cup 2026 fixtures, standings, and live scores without repeatedly opening a website or paying for a seasonal score app.
projects.description: WC26 is a practical native macOS side project I built as my first real Swift and SwiftUI app. I came into it from a senior frontend and full-stack background in React and TypeScript, using the project as a way to learn native app structure by shipping something genuinely useful for myself during the tournament season. The app runs from the menu bar using MenuBarExtra, fetches match data from the open-source `worldcup2026` API by Reza Rahiminia, normalizes raw match payloads into UI-friendly models, keeps live matches at the top, preserves stoppage-time formatting like 90'+8', and supports favorites, pinned live matches, notifications, refresh controls, start at login, and local preference persistence. It is intentionally small in scope, open source, and distributed unsigned because I did not want to pay the Apple developer fee for a fun side project.
highlights: Built as a native SwiftUI menu bar utility with fixtures, standings, team sheets, favorites, and live scores available in one click
Added a central AppViewModel, match normalization layer, and live-first ordering so messy API data becomes a cleaner real-time product experience
Improved timer parsing and notification handling to support meaningful details such as stoppage time, kickoff, goal, and full-time events
Stored user preferences locally for pinned matches, refresh interval, transparency, favorites, and notification behavior
Open-source project that credits the `worldcup2026` API provider directly and ships with honest unsigned-distribution tradeoffs

projects.title: zsk-ai-resume-api: FastAPI Backend for Portfolio Ask AI
projects.excerpt: A focused Python FastAPI backend that powers the portfolio Ask AI feature with Groq, strict prompt engineering, structured JSON responses, Redis caching, and production rate limiting.
projects.description: zsk-ai-resume-api is the separate backend service for my portfolio's Ask AI experience. It uses FastAPI, Pydantic settings, Groq's Llama 3.3 model, and a structured resume profile JSON to answer questions about my professional background. The backend includes strict prompt rules that keep answers scoped to my resume, prioritize professional experience before personal projects, return JSON-only responses, cache repeated questions in Upstash Redis, and enforce IP-based rate limiting in production while allowing unlimited local development. I also added compact profile context to reduce Groq token usage after seeing how quickly full-profile prompts can hit provider limits.
highlights: Built a Python FastAPI service with `/chat` and `/health` endpoints for the portfolio Ask AI feature
Integrated Groq Llama 3.3 with strict prompt engineering, JSON-only output, professional-experience-first evidence rules, and unrelated-question refusal
Used Upstash Redis for repeated-question caching, cache versioning, and IP-based production rate limiting
Added local development controls so rate limits can be disabled locally while remaining enabled in production
Reduced LLM token usage by compacting the resume profile before each Groq request instead of sending the full public JSON every time
Handled Groq provider rate-limit errors cleanly so the frontend can show a meaningful message instead of a generic failure

blog.title: I Ditched Axios for Ky And My Dependabot Finally Stopped Screaming
blog.excerpt: A personal breakdown of Fetch, Axios, and why Ky quietly became my go-to HTTP client in React.
blog.description: A practical comparison of Fetch, Axios, and Ky through the lens of bundle weight, retries, timeouts, TypeScript ergonomics, and the security cost of unnecessary dependencies.
highlights: Compares Fetch, Axios, and Ky through real React and TanStack Query usage
Breaks down Axios security incidents and supply-chain risk as a decision factor
Explains why Ky became the default request layer for modern React projects

blog.title: Context vs Redux Toolkit vs Zustand: Picking the Right State Tool for the Job
blog.excerpt: You don't need the most powerful state manager. You need the right one.
blog.description: A production-minded comparison of React Context, Redux Toolkit, and Zustand, focused on re-render behavior, boilerplate, team scaling, and the tradeoffs that matter months after launch.
highlights: Maps the strengths and weaknesses of Context, Redux Toolkit, and Zustand
Explains the Context re-render trap and why selector-based stores feel better at scale
Shows when scoped Zustand plus Context is the right hybrid pattern

blog.title: React Query vs SWR vs the `use` Hook: Why You're Fetching Data Wrong
blog.excerpt: You already know how to fetch data. What you're missing is everything that happens after.
blog.description: A production-focused comparison of raw fetch, SWR, React 19's `use` hook, and TanStack Query, centered on caching, mutations, race conditions, and why client-side data fetching is really a state synchronization problem.
highlights: Explains where raw fetch and Axios break down once caching, deduplication, and stale data enter the picture
Shows why the React 19 `use` hook is powerful in server components but limited as a client-side data fetching strategy
Compares SWR and TanStack Query through mutations, optimistic updates, DevTools, infinite queries, and real production tradeoffs

blog.title: You're Probably Using React Memoization Wrong (And So Was I)
blog.excerpt: Memoization is a performance tool, not a coding habit. Most of the time, the simpler version is the better version.
blog.description: A practical guide to `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo`, focused on when they solve real performance problems, when they add noise, and how React 19 changes the tradeoffs.
highlights: Explains when `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo` actually save meaningful work
Breaks down the reference equality traps that make manual memoization ineffective
Shows how React 19, `useDeferredValue`, and `useTransition` shift the performance conversation beyond blanket memoization

blog.title: React Compound Components: The Pattern That Makes Component APIs Actually Good
blog.excerpt: A long-form React architecture article on why prop-heavy components break down at scale and how compound components produce cleaner, more maintainable APIs.
blog.description: A practical deep dive into the compound components pattern in React, covering why monolithic prop-driven APIs become unmaintainable, how Context-based composition gives consumers layout control without losing shared state, and how to design the pattern correctly in TypeScript for real component libraries and design systems.
highlights: Builds Tabs and Accordion compound components from scratch with Context-based state sharing
Explains controlled vs uncontrolled APIs, namespaced TypeScript sub-components, and why Context beats `React.Children.map` here
Covers real-world usage, common mistakes, and lighter alternatives such as render props, config objects, and named slots

blog.title: React Virtualization: Fast Tables With Thousands of Rows
blog.excerpt: A practical, opinionated deep dive into React list and table virtualization focused on large datasets, real bottlenecks, and the tradeoffs behind adding windowing at all.
blog.description: This article treats virtualization as a DOM scaling problem first and a React implementation detail second. It starts with a DevTools-based workflow to confirm whether rendering cost is actually the bottleneck before reaching for a library, then walks through how windowing works under the hood, when it is the right call, when it is unnecessary, and how to implement it with TanStack Virtual, react-window, react-virtuoso, TanStack Table, and TanStack Query. It also covers variable row height strategies, infinite scroll, sticky headers, accessibility limitations, and the CSS and state-management mistakes that usually make virtualized tables feel fragile.
highlights: Explains virtualization from first principles: DOM recycling, scroll math, overscan, and why the browser usually fails before React does
Shows when to use virtualization and when to skip it for simpler options such as pagination, server-side filtering, or append-only lists
Includes practical implementations with TanStack Virtual, react-window, react-virtuoso, TanStack Table, and `useInfiniteQuery`
Covers variable-height rows, sticky header setup, refetch scroll-loss issues, and other failure modes that appear in real tables
Ends with the same rule as the rest of the series: measure first, then add complexity only when the evidence says you need it

blog.title: Concurrent Rendering in React: What It Actually Is, And When It's Just Hiding a Problem
blog.excerpt: Concurrent rendering is not multi-threading. It's React's way of rescheduling render work so urgent updates stay responsive.
blog.description: A technical deep dive into React's concurrent rendering model, focused on what Fiber actually enables, how urgent and non-urgent updates shape the API surface, when `startTransition`, `useTransition`, and `useDeferredValue` genuinely help, and when they are just masking a slower underlying problem.
highlights: Explains why concurrent rendering stays single-threaded and what Fiber actually makes interruptible
Breaks down `startTransition`, `useTransition`, and `useDeferredValue` through real UI cases and a clear decision table
Shows how concurrent rendering and Suspense fit together in data-heavy flows such as product detail navigation
Ends with a practical diagnosis framework so you measure the real bottleneck before reaching for any concurrent API

blog.title: React Reconciliation and Keys: What's Actually Happening When Your Component Re-Renders
blog.excerpt: Keys do not magically fix list bugs. They tell React which child identity should survive the next diff.
blog.description: A deep dive into React reconciliation focused on how the diffing heuristic actually matches elements, when a component updates versus remounts, why unstable keys corrupt stateful lists, and how Fiber makes selective reuse possible.
highlights: Explains React's two core diffing rules: type changes tear down subtrees, and same-type siblings are matched by key
Shows step by step why removing an item from a stateful list breaks under positional diffing and why index keys behave the same way
Clarifies the exact difference between a re-render and a remount, including what state survives and what resets
Connects reconciliation to Fiber internals, current versus work-in-progress trees, and practical DevTools debugging for unexpected remounts

blog.title: JavaScript Loops: Stop Using map() for Everything
blog.excerpt: Most loop mistakes are not style choices. They're cases where the code is saying one thing and doing another.
blog.description: A practical guide to choosing the right JavaScript loop based on intent, control flow, return value, async behavior, and readability, with concrete reasons to use `for`, `while`, `for...of`, `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `some`, `every`, and `flatMap`.
highlights: Separates imperative loops from functional array methods so the first decision is obvious
Explains the real tradeoffs behind `for`, `for...of`, `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, and `reduce` instead of treating them as style preferences
Calls out common production mistakes such as `forEach` with `async`/`await`, `map` for side effects, and `filter` where `some` or `find` should short-circuit

blog.title: Debugging React Apps Like a Senior Dev
blog.excerpt: Senior debugging starts before the first console.log. The difference is whether you form a hypothesis before touching anything.
blog.description: A practical, opinionated guide to debugging React applications systematically instead of randomly. Built around a four-part bug taxonomy, it covers React DevTools, the Profiler, `useEffect` failure patterns, re-render diagnostics, state and network debugging, memory leaks, production observability, and a six-step checklist for forming and testing hypotheses.
highlights: Opens with a four-category bug taxonomy: wrong state, wrong render logic, wrong effect, or wrong external input
Shows how to use React DevTools, the Profiler, why-did-you-render, and browser tooling to validate a debugging hypothesis fast
Covers the highest-frequency React bug classes including unstable effect dependencies, stale closures, render storms, cache confusion, and memory leaks
Includes practical production debugging guidance for source maps in Vite, Sentry with React error boundaries, feature flags, and structured console breadcrumbs

blog.title: Web Performance Beyond Lighthouse: What Actually Moves the Needle
blog.excerpt: A high Lighthouse score and a fast real-user experience are related, but they are not the same thing.
blog.description: A technical deep dive into modern web performance that separates lab scores from field reality, explains Core Web Vitals by mechanism, and focuses on the changes that materially improve what users actually feel across devices, networks, and full sessions.
